citation: John Moses and Joseph Kirkland, History of Chicago, Illinois, Volume I (Chicago and New York: Munsell & Co., 1895), 1,056 leaves. 'Aboriginal to Metropolitan', aided by eminent local writers. Chapters V and VI (printed pages 65-102) READ LINE BY LINE for the town before 1836; the two biographical sketches of men who were in the town before 1836 read in full; the remaining 900 leaves swept by surname and not read.
author: John Moses and Joseph Kirkland, with unsigned contributions by local writers; the biographical section in the volume's back half is separately written and separately paged in the contents
describes_date: Prehistory to 1895. Its 1830-1836 is Chapter VI, 'From Village to City - 1830 to 1837 - the Balloon Age' (leaves 107-141, printed pages 83-102), and its 1830s Chicago runs to about twelve printed pages.

transcribes.work: Chapters V and VI, 'Rudimentary - the Log Cabin Age' and 'From Village to City - 1830 to 1837 - the Balloon Age', leaves 89-141, printed pages 65-102
transcribes.note: A COMPILATION AT SIXTY YEARS' DISTANCE, and it quotes its own sources by name where it has them - Andreas, Colbert and Chamberlain, Latrobe's Rambler in North America, Granville Sproat's 1887 letter to the Tribune, John Wentworth in the Evening Journal of 2 March 1880 - which is what makes it usable and also what caps it. Where it names an earlier source this project should read that source instead; twenty-seven of the thirty-four claims here are recorded so that the comparison can be made without a re-read.

transcribes.work: The biographical sketches of Philip F. W. Peck (leaves 807-809, printed pages 569-571) and Philo Carpenter (leaves 810-811, printed pages 572-573)
transcribes.note: Obituary-grade lives written twenty-four and nine years after their subjects died, in a subscription county history whose biographical section exists to flatter. They are read here because both men were in Chicago before 1836 and this project holds both; their dates are worth testing and their superlatives are not evidence.

transcribes.work: The volume's own contents list of forty-seven biographies and its portrait list (leaves 21-23)
transcribes.note: The list is what answers T-0581's question and it needs no grading: it is a table of contents, and it either names a surname or it does not.

access_notes: Fetched 2026-09-05 from archive.org. THE ITEM IS THE PROJECT OWNER'S OWN UPLOAD, so the OCR read here is OCR of the very scan the deposit pointer names, not of a different copy. THE OWNER'S OPEN QUESTION ABOUT THE 'andr' FILE IS ANSWERED AND THE ANSWER IS THAT HE IS RIGHT TO WORRY: the item carries TWO complete works. Besides historyofchicago01mose.pdf it holds historyofchicago01andr.epub, historyofchicago01andr.pdf and a full set of andr-named derivatives, and the Internet Archive's own OCR of the andr files is a different book with a different title page. Only the mose-named derivatives were fetched, and only they are committed here; the andr text was not read and is not this source record. That is a finding for the owner, not a fault in the deposit: nothing in this project cites the andr files. TWO DERIVED TEXTS OF THE MOSE SCAN WERE COMPARED BEFORE ONE WAS CHOSEN - the djvu text (historyofchicago01mose_djvu.txt, 3.4 MB) and the hOCR search text - and the hOCR text was committed because the page index was emitted with it and therefore gives exact leaf boundaries where the djvu text gives none. THE OCR IS POOR AND THE CLAIMS SHOW IT: this scan renders 'The' as 'Тһе' with Cyrillic characters in dozens of places, breaks running heads across lines, and reads '1830' as '1550' in a chapter head. Every quote here is committed as printed, garbling included, because the verbatim gate checks the committed text and a tidied quote is invisible to it. No page render was made and none is committed; every claim is transcription_mediated and none is scan_verified.
what_it_supplies: the town's government on the scene date: the trustees elected in 1835 - Hiram Hugunin president, with W. Kimball, B. King, S. Jackson, E. B. Williams, F. C. Sherman, A. Lloyd and George W. Dole

the 1835 State census, taken between 1 September and December: 3,297 people, and with them a tally of the town's trades - forty-four stores, two book stores, four druggists, two silversmiths, two tin and copper manufactories, two printing offices, two breweries, one steam saw-mill, one iron foundry, four storage and forwarding houses, eight taverns, one lottery office, one bank, five churches, seven schools, twenty-two lawyers, fourteen physicians, a lyceum and reading room, and nine brick buildings among the year's new ones. IT IS TWO MONTHS AFTER THE SCENE DATE AND IS THEREFORE A CEILING FOR IT

the town's legal extent on the scene date: the act of 11 February 1835 taking in all land east of State street from Twelfth street to Chicago avenue, except the Fort Dearborn reservation, superseding the boundary of 6 November 1833
the twenty-eight men who voted at the first town election of 10 August 1833, printed as a footnote and naming Philo Carpenter among them

the trades advertised in the first numbers of the Chicago Democrat from 26 November 1833 - a list of nineteen firms and houses that CORROBORATES the newspaper this project already reads and does not replace it

corner placements for four buildings: George W. Dole's and P. F. W. Peck's first frame business buildings at the south-east corners of South Water/Dearborn and South Water/La Salle; J. S. C. Hogan's log storehouse, 45 by 18 feet, at the angle of Lake and South Water; and the Baptist church, a frame building on the corner of South Water and Franklin whose second storey held Sproat's school

Philo Carpenter's three successive drug stores - the leased log house near the river on the line of the future Lake street, the better quarters of the early winter of 1832, and the store he built in the summer of 1833 on what became South Water between La Salle and Fifth avenue

dimensions for two crossings: the first drawbridge at Dearborn street, 1834, 300 feet by sixteen with a double draw, built by Nelson R. Norton; and the south-branch bridge near Randolph, floating logs at first, built by Alanson H. and Charles Taylor from a $486.20 subscription of which the neighbouring Indians gave $200
the jail 'of logs well bolted together' at the north-west corner of the public square, and Samuel Miller's $12 estray pen beside it
a NEGATIVE date that matters: P. F. W. Peck's brick dwelling at the south-west corner of Washington and LaSalle was built in 1836 and is therefore NOT standing on 1 July 1835

two descriptions of the town's surface and fabric in 1833 - Latrobe's 'half a hundred clapboard houses' and Granville Sproat's mud 'half a leg deep' with a single plank for a sidewalk - both quoted by this volume from sources this project can read directly
arrival years for three cohorts of settlers (1832, 1833 and 1835) naming about forty men, most of whom this project already holds
what_it_does_not_supply: A BIOGRAPHY FOR MOST OF THE SURNAMES THE NEWBERRY INDEX POINTED AT, AND THIS IS T-0581'S ANSWER. The index names 66 Chicago and Cook County lead surnames citing this work. The volume carries a signed biography for eleven of them, and only three of those eleven men - Philo Carpenter, John Dean Caton and Philip F. W. Peck - were in Chicago before 1836. The other thirty-six sketches are of men who made their names after 1848. TWELVE OF THE 66 SURNAMES DO NOT OCCUR IN VOLUME 1 AT ALL: blodget, caapbell, chamberlin, chancy, franke, gardiner, gunn, heal, jacobe, mattoson, nlan and obrien - and several of those are the Newberry cards' own OCR garbling rather than real names

any of volume 2. Volume 2 (historyofchicagov2mose) has not been uploaded to the owner's account, has not been fetched, and is not read. The Newberry cards that cite 'Moses and Kirkland' do not say which volume, so this reading closes half the question
a household. The volume names men and trades; it never gives a household composition, a wife's or child's name in the 1830s narrative, or a residence for anybody in the town in 1835

a resolution of its own contradiction about the first brick building. Chapter VI gives it to John Noble in 1833, built by Alanson Sweet and William Worthingham on the North Side; the Peck sketch gives it to P. F. W. Peck in 1836 and calls it 'the first structure of that material put up in the town'. This pass records both and resolves neither
a page image, a plan, a measured elevation or any dimension of an 1835 building beyond Hogan's 45 by 18 feet and the Dearborn drawbridge's 300 by 16

an independent source for most of what it says about the 1830s. Where the volume is at its most useful it is quoting Andreas, Colbert and Chamberlain, Latrobe, Sproat's 1887 letter or the Chicago Democrat - all of which outrank it and three of which this project already holds
anything about the ground. Nothing here touches data/datum.json, which is derived from committed ground control; the Sproat mud passage is a description of a street in one autumn and is not a grade
note: READ FOR T-0581, WHICH CAME OFF THE NEWBERRY GENEALOGICAL INDEX (T-0570) - 76 of that index's 581 Chicago and Cook County cards cite this work, and it was the largest Chicago work the index pointed at that this project did not hold. IT NOW HOLDS HALF OF IT. The value turns out to be narrow and real: twelve printed pages of 1830s narrative, dense with corners and dates, plus two lives of pre-1836 men. THE INDEX'S PREMISE DOES NOT SURVIVE THE READING, and that is worth saying plainly - a Newberry card citing 'Moses and Kirkland' for a surname is a card about a FAMILY, and this volume's biographies are of Gilded Age Chicagoans, so a lead surname reaching this work almost never reaches an 1835 person through it. NOTHING IN data/residents/, data/households/, data/businesses/, data/structures/ OR data/assets/ WAS EDITED BY THIS PASS. The placements at bk_mk1_001, bk_mk1_005, bk_mk1_015, bk_mk1_033 and the negative date at bk_mk1_031 are OFFERED to the structures and businesses layers and must be adopted, if at all, in those layers' own PRs under the ratified ladder - which is what T-0581 asks for. Four open tickets are touched and none is decided here: T-0396 (Newberry and Dole's partner), T-0407 (Matthias Mason/Nason the blacksmith), T-0412 (P. Pruyne & Co.'s store) and the Green Tree tavern's keeper, whom this volume gives as David Clock in 1833 and whose building it gives to James Kinzie.
